result.abstractText: Partial reprogramming by cyclic expression of Yamanaka factors has been proposed as a rejuvenation strategy, yet evaluating tissue-specific responses and potential risks remains challenging. Here, we reanalyzed RNA-seq data from the liver, kidney, and spleen of aged mice subjected to seven months of partial reprogramming. We used the Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) framework to estimate adverse and beneficial signatures, assessed functional changes via gene set enrichment analysis and deconvoluted bulk RNA-seq data to estimate differences in cell type proportion. In the liver and kidney, partial reprogramming suppressed age-activated immune and inflammatory processes, while activating age-suppressed metabolic and catabolic pathways. In the spleen, cell cycle, DNA replication, and DNA damage response programs were prominent, indicative of increased proliferative activity, and cell type deconvolution showed increased proportions of megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor cells and decreased proportions of natural killer cells, while AOPs flagged a potential risk of sustained genomic and proliferative stress. Based on the existing AOP framework, we did not find any enriched Key Events in the kidney (reprogrammed vs. old). In the liver, AOP analysis identified pathways regulated in opposition to liver steatosis, indicated by activation of nuclear receptor signaling (Ppara, Pparg) and restoration of fatty-acid oxidation and metabolism. Our findings highlight tissue-specific responses to partial reprogramming and emphasize the need for larger, controlled studies to clarify physiological outcomes and safety.

result.abstractText: Aging is associated with functional decline and reduced regenerative capacity in the brain, is also the strongest risk factor for ischemic stroke, which remains a leading cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide, and is associated with impaired functional recovery. Here, we investigated whether short-term partial cellular reprogramming through cyclic expression of Yamanaka factors (OSKM) in a Tet-ON mouse model under Rosa-26 promoter has any impact on ischemic damage in aged mice. To assess ischemic resilience, mice underwent permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion (pMCAo). Forty-eight hours after ischemia, OSKM-induced mice displayed significantly smaller damaged area compared with wild-type controls, accompanied by improved neurological scores and enhanced performance in the tightrope test, suggesting preserved sensorimotor abilities. Notably, myelin integrity was preserved in OSKM-treated mice, as shown by Black-Gold staining and stable MAG and MBP expression, whereas wild-type mice exhibited pronounced demyelination. Given the role of oligodendrocytes in myelin maintenance, we quantified the abundance of their different populations. OSKM induction significantly increased total oligodendrocytes (Olig2<sup>+</sup>) and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (PDGFRα<sup>+</sup>) following ischemia, suggesting an enhanced reparative response. Moreover, partial reprogramming preserved neuronal density in the ischemic cortex and prevented the marked astrocytic activation observed in wild-type mice, while microglial responses remained comparable across genotypes. These findings demonstrate that cyclic partial reprogramming in aged mice reduces ischemic damage, highlighting OSKM induction as a promising strategy for enhancing brain resilience during cerebrovascular accidents.
